s01.1.text: A large language model is one mathematical function.

s01.2.text: It reads a sequence of tokens and returns a probability for every possible next token.

s01.3.text: That is the whole interface: text in, a distribution over the next token out.

s01.4.text: LLaMA-3-Lite is a compact, from-scratch model built in the LLaMA-3 style.

s01.5.text: Sixteen decoder blocks, a model dimension of one thousand twenty-four, and about five hundred fifteen million parameters.

s01.6.text: The same model width runs through all sixteen blocks.

s01.7.text: Take the sentence on screen: The cat sat on the mat.

s01.8.text: Six tokens, six IDs, and one question: what comes next?

s01.9.text: One token walks in as an ID and walks out as a probability over the whole vocabulary.

s01.10.text: Follow that walk from raw text to the sampling loop, one stage at a time.

s01.11.text: Each stage exists to fix a specific problem the previous stage leaves open.

s01.12.text: The loop at the end is what turns one prediction into a paragraph.

s02.1.text: Before any architecture, ask what the model is trained to do.

s02.2.text: The objective is next-token cross-entropy, plus a small z-loss at one ten-thousandth.

s02.3.text: Training shows the model real text with the next token hidden.

s02.4.text: The model assigns that hidden token a probability.

s02.5.text: When the probability is low, training adjusts the weights to raise it.

s02.6.text: That adjustment is the whole of learning: every weight moves to make real text more likely.

s02.7.text: Next-token training needs no extra manual labels: no sentiment tags, no answers, no rules.

s02.8.text: The loss measures surprise: how low the model's probability was for the true token.

s02.9.text: Pushing surprise down is what shapes the five hundred fifteen million parameters.

s02.10.text: From that single objective, grammar, style and world knowledge settle into the weights.

s02.11.text: Nothing in the code says what a noun is.

s02.12.text: Training runs that prediction at every position in parallel.

s02.13.text: Generation instead reveals one new token at a time.

s02.14.text: The structure you are about to see is the machinery that makes the prediction possible.

s02.15.text: Each piece is there because the objective demands it.

s03.1.text: Text cannot enter a matrix multiply, so the tokenizer goes first.

s03.2.text: It splits text into subword pieces from a vocabulary of one hundred twenty-eight thousand two hundred fifty-six tokens.

s03.3.text: The scheme is byte-pair encoding: the most frequent character pairs merge into new tokens.

s03.4.text: Building it starts from single characters and keeps merging the most common pair.

s03.5.text: Common words stay whole, and rare words break into smaller pieces the model has seen before.

s03.6.text: Characters alone would make sequences far too long; whole words alone would explode the vocabulary.

s03.7.text: Subwords sit in between and cover any input, including words the model has never seen.

s03.8.text: Their IDs come straight from the vocabulary table.

s03.9.text: The word cat becomes eight thousand four hundred fifteen; the word mat becomes five thousand six hundred thirty-four.

s03.10.text: Each ID is just a row number; it carries no meaning of its own.

s03.11.text: The tokenizer knows nothing about cats.

s03.12.text: Its only job is to cut text into pieces the model has a row for.

s03.13.text: The config lists one hundred twenty-eight thousand rows; the tokenizer holds two hundred fifty-six more.

s03.14.text: The embedding table sizes itself to the tokenizer, not to the config.

s04.1.text: An ID is only a row number; the row it points to carries the meaning.

s04.2.text: That lookup is the embedding matrix, one row per vocabulary item.

s04.3.text: Each row holds one thousand twenty-four numbers, so every token becomes a vector of that length.

s04.4.text: A lookup is all it takes: the ID picks the row, and the row becomes the token's vector.

s04.5.text: There is no computation here yet, only a learned table.

s04.6.text: Training can move these rows so tokens used in similar ways land near each other.

s04.7.text: This is how it can learn semantic geometry: directions that carry meaning.

s04.8.text: An illustrative sketch might place cat near kitten and far from car.

s04.9.text: Because the table is learned, it embeds each token by how that token is used.

s04.10.text: The vector is a point in one thousand twenty-four dimensions, far too many to picture at once.

s04.11.text: Two dimensions stand in for the rest whenever the screen shows a sketch.

s04.12.text: From this point on the model sees only vectors, never characters.

s04.13.text: From here, each token carries its vector through all sixteen blocks.

s04.14.text: That carried vector is called the residual stream.

s04.15.text: Inside a block, attention and SwiGLU each read a normalized copy of the stream.

s04.16.text: Each writes its result back onto the stream by simple addition.

s04.17.text: This pre-norm shape is the structure of every decoder block.

s04.18.text: A last RMSNorm at the output cleans that same stream before scoring.

s04.19.text: A separate, untied table of the same kind runs at the output, as you will see.

s05.1.text: A single vector knows its own meaning and nothing about its neighbors.

s05.2.text: The next problem is context: how a token learns what surrounds it.

s05.3.text: Self-attention solves this in one layer, by letting every token look back at the tokens before it.

s05.4.text: Each vector is projected three times: into a query, a key, and a value.

s05.5.text: The query is what a token asks for.

s05.6.text: The key is what a token offers for matching.

s05.7.text: The value is the information a token hands over once it is chosen.

s05.8.text: All three projections are learned matrices, multiplied into the stream.

s05.9.text: A query takes a dot product with every key in the sequence.

s05.10.text: A large dot product means similar direction, long length, or both.

s05.11.text: Each dot product fills one cell of the score matrix.

s05.12.text: Those scores are divided by the square root of the key dimension.

s05.13.text: Without scaling, scores grow with the dimension and the softmax saturates.

s05.14.text: Scaling controls that growth and keeps the softmax away from saturation.

s05.15.text: The matrix on screen is the map of who will listen to whom.

s06.1.text: Scores are still raw numbers; they need to become weights.

s06.2.text: A causal mask hides the future from every query.

s06.3.text: A token may attend to itself and to earlier tokens, never later ones.

s06.4.text: Training never allows a token to read the answer it is being asked to predict.

s06.5.text: Masked scores are pushed to negative infinity before the softmax runs.

s06.6.text: Softmax turns the remaining scores into positive weights that sum to one.

s06.7.text: Look at the row for the word sat on screen.

s06.8.text: It places zero point eight six of its weight on cat.

s06.9.text: The masked future cell holds zero.

s06.10.text: The weights then blend the value vectors into a single output.

s06.11.text: The output is a weighted average of past values, so it stays near their neighborhood.

s06.12.text: Each token leaves attention carrying a summary of its own past.

s06.13.text: This whole computation runs eight times in parallel, one per head.

s06.14.text: Query projections are per head, but keys and values are shared by pairs of heads.

s06.15.text: The eight outputs are concatenated and multiplied by one output matrix.

s06.16.text: The result is written back into the residual stream.

s07.1.text: Attention as written cannot see word order: shuffle the tokens and the outputs shuffle to match.

s07.2.text: The scores only see vectors, and the vectors so far carry meaning without position.

s07.3.text: So the next piece adds position without touching the meaning.

s07.4.text: Rotary embeddings fix this by rotating query and key vectors according to position.

s07.5.text: Each vector is split into pairs of dimensions, sixty-four pairs per head.

s07.6.text: Each pair is read as a point in two dimensions, or as a complex number.

s07.7.text: Position m rotates every pair by an angle of m times a base frequency.

s07.8.text: The rotation matrix on screen is the pair version of that turn.

s07.9.text: Different pairs turn at different speeds.

s07.10.text: Fast pairs pin down nearby structure; slow pairs mark long-range position.

s07.11.text: The fastest pair shown completes a full turn in about six point three tokens.

s07.12.text: When a rotated query meets a rotated key, their rotations combine into one relative turn.

s07.13.text: So the positional part of their dot product depends on the distance between them.

s07.14.text: Content still shapes the score; position adds only how far apart the two tokens sit.

s07.15.text: With theta at five hundred thousand, the slowest pairs stay smooth across two thousand forty-eight tokens.

s07.16.text: Theta sets the slowest wavelength; a larger theta pushes it further.

s08.1.text: One Lite detail lands between projection and rotation.

s08.2.text: Queries and keys each pass through RMSNorm before RoPE is applied.

s08.3.text: This controls the scale of each query and key, so the logits stay well behaved.

s08.4.text: The norm runs per head, on each query and key vector on its own.

s08.5.text: Each layer has one shared gain of one hundred twenty-eight numbers for queries, and one for keys.

s08.6.text: The point of the step is training stability, at a tiny parameter cost.

s08.7.text: LLaMA 3 itself has no QK-norm; the step is a Lite addition.

s09.1.text: Attention during training sees the whole sentence at once.

s09.2.text: Generation is different: the model writes one token, then the next, then the next.

s09.3.text: Each new token still has to see everything before it.

s09.4.text: Recomputing every past key and value at every step would waste work.

s09.5.text: An inference-time optimization can store those vectors in a KV cache.

s09.6.text: Each layer stores two vectors per token for every key-value head.

s09.7.text: With sixteen layers and four key-value heads, one token costs sixteen thousand three hundred eighty-four stored numbers.

s09.8.text: That count assumes one hundred twenty-eight numbers per head.

s09.9.text: At two thousand forty-eight tokens of context, the cache passes thirty-three million numbers.

s09.10.text: The cache is a growing memory cost at inference time.

s09.11.text: LLaMA-3-Lite runs eight query heads and four key-value heads.

s09.12.text: Each key-value head is shared by two query heads.

s09.14.text: Four key-value heads halve the cache against eight, while the math of attention stays the same.

s09.15.text: The attention operation is unchanged, though a smaller key-value set can still change model quality.

s10.1.text: Two sublayers sit in every block; attention is the first.

s10.2.text: The second is a feed-forward network applied to each token on its own.

s10.3.text: Attention mixes tokens; the feed-forward works on each vector in isolation.

s10.4.text: It widens the vector from one thousand twenty-four to four thousand ninety-six, then compresses it back.

s10.5.text: The wide middle gives the block room to transform features between the two widths.

s10.6.text: Count the parameters and the feed-forward dominates: over twelve million per block against about three million for attention.

s10.7.text: LLaMA gates this expansion with SwiGLU.

s10.8.text: The wide layer splits into two parallel paths: a gate path and an up path.

s10.9.text: Both paths start from the same input vector.

s10.10.text: The gate path passes through the SiLU activation, which is x times its own sigmoid.

s10.11.text: Near zero, SiLU passes about half the input; large positive inputs pass nearly unchanged.

s10.12.text: Element by element, the gate path scales the up path.

s10.13.text: The gate can shrink a feature, pass it unchanged, or amplify it.

s10.14.text: Only the product of the two paths flows onward.

s10.15.text: Multiplicative gating lets one path decide how much of the other to keep.

s10.16.text: A final matrix projects the result back into the residual stream.

s11.1.text: After sixteen blocks, one last RMSNorm settles the stream.

s11.2.text: A separate, untied matrix scores all one hundred twenty-eight thousand two hundred fifty-six candidates.

s11.3.text: Each score, called a logit, is one dot product between the final vector and one candidate row.

s11.4.text: This unembedding table is as large as the embedding table: about one hundred thirty-one million parameters in each.

s11.5.text: Together, the two tables hold just over half of the model.

s11.6.text: Large logits mean the candidate fits the context well.

s11.7.text: A softmax turns the logits into probabilities over the whole vocabulary.

s11.8.text: Sampling picks one token, and that token is appended to the context.

s11.9.text: The full network then runs again for the next one.

s11.10.text: One forward pass per generated token; that is the generation loop.

s11.11.text: A KV cache would keep past keys and values, so each new pass computes only the newest token.

s11.12.text: Without one, every step re-reads the whole sequence; this code does exactly that.

s11.13.text: What began as one function on a table of numbers now writes a paragraph.

s12.1.text: Walk the whole path once more, from text to a sampled token.

s12.2.text: The tokenizer cuts the sentence into six pieces with integer IDs.

s12.3.text: The embedding table turns each ID into a vector of one thousand twenty-four numbers.

s12.4.text: The residual stream carries those vectors through sixteen blocks.

s12.5.text: In each block, RMSNorm controls scale, attention mixes context, and the gated feed-forward rewrites features.

s12.6.text: Rotary embeddings keep the order of the tokens visible through all of it.

s12.7.text: Grouped-query attention keeps the cache affordable; QK-norm keeps the logits stable.

s12.8.text: The unembedding table scores every candidate, and sampling takes one.

s12.9.text: About five hundred fifteen million parameters, and one function from tokens to probabilities.
